capabilities.name: Google advertising ID (AAID/GAID)
capabilities.plain: A resettable Google ID apps use for ads, which the person can delete, giving apps zeros.
capabilities.meaning: The cross-app join key on Android: install attribution, retargeting, frequency capping. Users can reset or delete it; kids apps must not send it.

limits.headline: Can use a resettable Google ad ID to link your activity across apps
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the app or its ad tool starts
can: Join your activity across apps that use the same ad ID
Count installs, show retargeting ads, and limit how often you see an ad
Give a string of zeros once you delete the ID (Android 12 and later)
cannot: Use the ID after you delete it in Settings, Privacy, Ads
Send it to third parties from a kids app
Follow you after you reset it, as the ID changes
Be used on iPhone; the Apple equivalent is the IDFA
limits.differs: Android only. iPhone uses the IDFA, which needs the tracking prompt.

story.what_it_is: A reset button ID on Android that apps and ad networks use to recognize your phone.

marketing.name: Advertising ID
marketing.pitch: A user resettable ID for advertising that you can delete at any time in settings.

story.for_you: You normally do not see it. In Settings you can reset it or delete it, which turns it into a row of zeros and makes ads less targeted.
story.for_makers: It is the main cross app join key on Android: ads show who clicked, who installed and who came back. Makers use it for install attribution, retargeting and frequency caps, and kids apps must not send it.

use_cases.example: You click a game ad, install, and the ad network matches the ID to prove its ad worked.
A game shows a bonus offer to players who came from a certain campaign and who still have the ID.
A shop retargets you with a banner for the shoes you left in the cart.
An ad network caps a user to three views a day by remembering the ID.
A growth team joins the ID in several apps to see how often users switch.
A fraud tool spots a device with many fake installs using the same ID pattern.

story.android_note: Android lets you reset or delete the ID, and Android 13 needs the AD_ID permission.
story.ios_note: iOS has the IDFA instead, behind the App Tracking Transparency prompt.

technical_bounds: Zero value after delete or without AD_ID
Apps for kids must not send it
Wear OS and other form factors vary

legit_uses: Attribution and ads for consenting users

AD_ID permission declared; missing declaration returns zeros for apps targeting 13+
Privacy Sandbox wound down; ad ID unchanged

platform.store_policy: Play Ads policy: use the ad ID for advertising instead of other IDs; Families: must not transmit
platform.note: Returns 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 after deletion (Android 12+). No Privacy Sandbox replacement is coming: the Oct 2025 wind-down left the ad ID as the main cross-app identifier.

capabilities.name: AdAttributionKit re-engagement conversions
capabilities.plain: Measures whether an ad brought an existing user back into the app.
capabilities.meaning: SKAN could only count new installs. Re-engagement attribution lets advertisers measure retargeting without an IDFA.

limits.user_action: You tap an ad, then open the app you already installed
can: Tell the advertiser an ad led you to reopen the app
Count it without an ad ID
Work with overlapping windows from iOS 18.4
cannot: Name you or give your device ID in the report
Report right away; there are delays
Work on Android; there is no matching feature
Run more than one window at a time before iOS 18.4

story.what_it_is: Apple's way to measure whether an ad brought an existing user back into an app.

marketing.name: AdAttributionKit
marketing.pitch: Measure installs and re-engagement with privacy preserving reports.

story.for_you: You tap an ad for an app you already have and it opens. Apple quietly counts that the ad worked, without telling the advertiser who you are.
story.for_makers: Old SKAdNetwork could only count new installs. Re-engagement lets advertisers measure retargeting campaigns, so they can win back lapsed users without the IDFA.

use_cases.example: A lapsed player sees 'come back and get a free pack' and returning is counted for the campaign.
A shopper taps a sale ad for an app they have and the retailer sees that the ad led to a return.
A promo for a free ride makes a dormant rider open the app, and the ad network gets the credit.
A streaming service measures how many ads brought back cancelled subscribers.
An ad network reports re-engagement conversions in coarse values after delays.
A growth team compares the lift from a re-engagement campaign against a control group.

story.android_note: The Android counterpart for re-engagement was part of the retired Attribution Reporting plan.
story.ios_note: Supported by AdAttributionKit from iOS 17.4.

Same crowd anonymity limits

capabilities.name: AdAttributionKit (iOS 17.4)
capabilities.plain: Apple's successor to SKAdNetwork that also covers re-engagement and alternative app stores.
capabilities.meaning: A privacy-preserving way for ad networks to measure installs, reopens and re-downloads. Compatible with SKAN postbacks, adds marketplaces beyond the App Store.

limits.user_action: You tap an ad, then install or reopen the app
can: Tell the ad network an ad led to an install, reopen or re-download
Work with alternative app stores
Send a copy of the report to the developer, if set up
Add the country code and set up windows from iOS 18.4
cannot: Give your name or device ID
Report right away or in detail; reports are delayed and coarse
Work on Android; the Android version was retired
limits.differs: iPhone only (iOS 17.4 and later). Android's matching system was retired.

story.what_it_is: Apple's newer privacy friendly ad measurement system, replacing SKAdNetwork.

marketing.name: AdAttributionKit
marketing.pitch: Measure ad conversions, with user privacy built in and support for alternative marketplaces.

story.for_you: You see nothing. Apple sends delayed, noisy reports to advertisers that an ad led to an install, without sharing your name or device ID.
story.for_makers: It tells ad networks which campaign worked while hiding which person did it. It adds re-downloads, re-engagement and alternative app marketplaces, and works alongside SKAN postbacks.

use_cases.example: An ad network checks that a campaign drove 200 installs and gets the answer three days later.
A studio sees which of its ads bring paying players, using a coarse value after the first day.
A retailer measures how many app installs came from a short video ad.
In the EU an alternative app store uses the same kit to measure installs from ads.
A marketing team compares results across ad networks in one report.
Signed reports stop fake networks from claiming credit for installs they did not drive.

story.android_note: Google's matching Privacy Sandbox attribution plan was retired in October 2025.
story.ios_note: Added in iOS 17.4 and compatible with SKAN postbacks.

technical_bounds: Postbacks signed by Apple
Crowd anonymity applies
Dev beta postbacks for testing

Overlapping re-engagement windows, configurable attribution windows and cooldown, country code in postbacks

capabilities.name: In-app consent platforms (TCF/CMP)
capabilities.plain: A consent screen the developer shows (in addition to the OS prompt) for EEA, UK and some US laws.
capabilities.meaning: Recorded consent decides what ad SDKs may do. Since 2024 Google requires a certified CMP for ads in the EEA. On iOS it adds a second prompt beside ATT, which Italy called double consent.

limits.headline: Can show an extra consent screen on top of the phone prompt
limits.user_action: You see a Consent screen the first time you open the app, often in the EU or UK

Store your answer on the phone
Tell its ad tools what you agreed to
Show again later if you change your mind
cannot: Skip the screen when Google needs a certified one for EEA ads
Count as your consent if the answer is not recorded
Replace the phone's own prompt; on iPhone you may see two
limits.reach_label: Your choice, passed to the app

story.what_it_is: The extra consent screen an app shows, for privacy laws, on top of the phone's own prompt.
story.for_you: You see a screen asking you to accept or manage cookies and ad choices in an app, often before the app opens. Your answer is saved and sent to ad partners.
story.for_makers: Laws like GDPR require consent before personal ad data is used. Makers use a CMP so ad SDKs only do what the saved choice allows, and Google requires it for ads in the EEA.

use_cases.example: A news app asks you to consent to personalized ads before showing articles.
A free game shows a consent form at first launch, then loads ads based on your answer.
An ad SDK reads the saved consent string and serves non personalized ads when you say no.
A social app offers separate toggles for ads, analytics and personalization.
A retailer stores your consent so it can prove it asked, for audits.
A product team measures how many users accept and tunes the wording.

story.android_note: Android has no system consent screen. Apps use a CMP.
story.ios_note: On iOS the CMP appears beside the ATT prompt, which Apple allows if it is not misleading.

technical_bounds: Two prompts on iOS
Consent must precede SDK init in EEA

history.change: Certified CMP required for ads in EEA and UK (Jan 2024)
Italy fines Apple over double consent

platform.store_policy: Google EU user consent policy; Play Families
platform.api_surface: Google UMP SDK, TCF 2.2 strings in app storage
platform.note: Consent string stored in SharedPreferences (IABTCF_).

capabilities.meaning: Ties activity to a Meta account for ads. Can send hashed email or phone (advanced matching). Logs events even for signed-out Facebook users.

story.what_it_is: Meta's code library that reports installs and in app actions so Facebook can match them to ads.

marketing.name: Facebook SDK for iOS and Android
marketing.pitch: Add Facebook Login, sharing and app events to measure ads and understand your audience.

story.for_you: You never see it. If you used Facebook or clicked a Meta ad, the app might tell Meta you opened it, bought something or reached a level.
story.for_makers: Meta uses the events to match purchases to ads and to build audiences. Advanced matching can send hashed email or phone, and the SDK can log events even for people signed out of Facebook.

use_cases.example: A game reports 'level 10 reached' so Meta can find more players like your best ones.
A store app reports a purchase so the advertiser sees which Instagram ad drove the sale.
A login button lets you sign in with Facebook and shares your name and email.
Advanced matching sends a hashed email so Meta can join an app purchase to your account.
A dating app counts how many installs came from video ads on Instagram.
Privacy researchers found the SDK sending data before consent in some apps.

risks: Joins app use to your Facebook profile

story.ios_note: On iOS, SKAN and ATT limit how much Meta can link, but hashed email matching still works.

technical_bounds: Needs consent for ads use under GDPR
Events can be disabled
Privacy manifest and signature required

Limited Login for Facebook Login without ATT

capabilities.name: Fingerprinting ban and ATT enforcement
capabilities.plain: Apple forbids deriving a device identity from signals to track someone who said no under ATT.
capabilities.meaning: Stops apps and SDKs from rebuilding an ID from IP, model, locale and similar signals after the person refused tracking. It is enforced mainly at App Review and by required reason API gating.

limits.headline: Can't rebuild your identity from phone details after you refuse tracking on iPhone
limits.user_action: Nothing. You said no on the tracking prompt; Apple enforces it in review
can: Use ordinary details for fraud and app function, within Apple's rules
Measure results in groups without naming you
Use IP addresses on Android; Play does not ban it
cannot: Combine IP, model and language to build an ID on iPhone
Hide it behind a consent banner
Use blocked tracking sites after you said no
Pass App Review if found doing it
limits.differs: Apple bans fingerprinting even with a banner. Google Play does not ban matching and now allows IP use in ads.

story.what_it_is: Apple's rule that bans rebuilding a device ID from small clues after you say no to tracking.

marketing.name: App Review Guidelines, Data use and sharing
marketing.pitch: Apps must not derive data from a device to identify a user who declined tracking.

story.for_you: You do not see anything. It is a rule that says: if you tap 'Ask App Not to Track', the app may not secretly follow you anyway using your phone model, language and IP address.
story.for_makers: Makers who use fingerprinting risk rejection. Apple enforces it at App Review and through required reason APIs, so ad networks moved to clearly permitted measures like SKAN.

use_cases.example: An ad network that mixed IP and model to rebuild an ID could see its apps pulled.
A game studio drops a probabilistic attribution tool to avoid a rejection.
A measurement firm limits itself to consented IDs and anonymous aggregates.
Fraud teams may use signals to stop abuse, but not to track people for ads.
A retailer is told to remove a script that built a device profile from signals.
A developer reads the guideline and rewrites its tracker to use only IDFV inside its own apps.

story.android_note: Android has no equal rule, but Google Play bans abusive fingerprinting for ads on kids apps.
story.ios_note: Applied mainly through App Review and the privacy manifest process.

technical_bounds: Review rejection for SDKs that fingerprint
NSPrivacyTrackingDomains blocked at the network layer when ATT is not granted (declared domains only)
Enforcement is largely review time, not runtime

history.change: Apple tells developers ATT cannot be bypassed by fingerprinting
Required reason APIs announced to curb signals used for fingerprinting
Required reason API reasons enforced for new uploads (1 May 2024)

Apple: Describing use of required reason API

limits.user_action: Nothing. It starts when the app opens and runs while you use it
can: Count sessions, screens and purchases for the developer
Give each install its own ID that resets on reinstall (Android)
Link to Google Ads and BigQuery reports
Run with the developer ID only on iPhone, without tracking permission

Use Google Signals on iPhone without consent
Keep the same ID after you clear the app data or reinstall (Android)

story.what_it_is: Google's free tool that counts what people do in an app and links it to Google Ads.

marketing.name: Google Analytics for Firebase
marketing.pitch: Free, unlimited event reporting that shows how people use your app and what drives growth.

story.for_you: You never see it. It logs each time you open the app, how long you stay and what you tap, and gives your install a long random ID.
story.for_makers: It builds an event stream per install and links it to Google Ads and BigQuery. Teams use it to find drop off points, test ideas and send audiences to ads, and it is free, so nearly every app has it.

use_cases.example: A studio sees that 40 percent of players quit at level 3, so it makes the level easier.
A retail app tracks how many users add to cart but never pay, then sends a reminder.
A running app measures which workout types people finish and which they skip.
Google Ads uses the events to find similar users and judge which ads bring buyers.
A video app measures play time and tests a new recommendation row.
A team ties crashes to a version using the same install ID and fixes the bug.

story.android_note: On Android it can also use the advertising ID if the app has the AD_ID permission.
story.ios_note: On iOS it respects ATT for IDFA and otherwise uses an app instance ID.

Data retention 2 or 14 months default

story.for_makers: Google already knows the click, the Play install and the account, so the SDK only has to add what happens in the app. That closes the loop with no third party tool, and feeds Google's bidding with real results.

use_cases.example: A studio runs an app campaign and sees which ads bring players who spend money in week one.
A retailer measures how many YouTube viewers install the app and buy within a day.
A ride app measures first ride completions after an ad install, to set its bids.
A bank counts approved accounts from ads and bids more for similar people.
Google's automated bidding learns to show ads to people like past buyers.
A growth team sends the same events to Firebase and Ads and compares the two reports.

story.for_you: You notice it as better battery life overnight. It may also delay a message or an alarm by some minutes. Only high priority messages, exact alarms and some services get through.
story.for_makers: Makers must plan around it: they use high priority push, exact alarms and foreground services for urgent work. Some apps ask users to switch off battery limits, which Google discourages.

use_cases.example: A chat app receives a message through a high priority push while the phone sleeps.
A calendar app rings a meeting alarm on time using an exact alarm.
A step tracker batches data and syncs when the phone wakes.
A game that wants energy refilled uses a timed notification rather than a background job.
A bad app asks you to turn off battery limits so it can keep running at night.
A security camera app uses high priority alerts to wake the phone when motion is seen.

story.android_note: This is Android only, with Doze and App Standby buckets that decide how often an app can run.
story.ios_note: iPhone has no Doze, but it limits background work through its own scheduler.

technical_bounds: Maintenance windows lengthen over time
FCM high priority is the sanctioned wake path

abuse: Evading Doze with battery opt-out prompts

history.change: Doze on the go (screen off, moving)

refs.label: Android: Optimize for Doze and App Standby

platform.prompt_ui: Settings > Battery > Unrestricted removes the app from optimization
platform.persistence: Doze deepens over hours; maintenance windows get longer
platform.store_policy: Play: ignore battery optimizations only for apps whose core function breaks otherwise
platform.note: While-idle alarms limited to 7 per hour; network and wakelocks suspended except in maintenance windows

capabilities.name: Why the process ended (exit reasons)
capabilities.plain: Apps can read why they were killed: Android ApplicationExitInfo, iOS MetricKit exit metrics.
capabilities.meaning: Lets apps and SDKs learn whether the system, the user or a crash ended a session. Android 17 adds a memory limiter reason; it also exposes behavior to the person's device.

limits.headline: Can learn why the system last ended the app, such as low memory
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens the next time the app starts or a report arrives
can: List recent reasons the app was ended on Android, such as low memory or you swiping it away
Get exit counts by reason on iPhone through MetricKit
Fix crashes and memory problems with the reports
cannot: See why other apps ended
See your data or activity
Get iPhone reports faster than about once per 24 hours
limits.differs: Android lists recent exits one by one. iPhone gives counts about once a day.

story.what_it_is: An app can read why it was closed: by you, by a crash or by the system.

marketing.name: ApplicationExitInfo
marketing.pitch: Android tells apps why a previous process ended, such as a crash or low memory.

marketing.name: MetricKit
marketing.pitch: Apple reports crash and exit data to apps so they can fix problems.

story.for_you: You do not see it. When an app crashes or gets killed, it can learn why and later fix the bug. You may see fewer crashes over time.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to find crashes, out of memory kills and battery problems. It also shows how you use the phone. Patterns of exits can serve as a quiet device profile.

use_cases.example: A developer sees that many users hit a memory kill on one phone model and fixes it.
A game studio finds that a level crashes older phones and lowers its graphics.
A video app notes that the system closed it during long playback and reduces memory use.
A run tracker learns that the phone killed it mid run and starts a foreground service.
An analytics kit stores exit patterns to tell phones apart.
A security tool notices repeated kills that match a tampering attempt.

risks: Shows how you use the phone
story.android_note: Android 17 adds a memory limiter reason to ApplicationExitInfo.
story.ios_note: iPhone reports exit data in aggregate through MetricKit.

technical_bounds: Android keeps a short history
iOS gives daily aggregates only

history.change: App memory limits report REASON_OTHER with MemoryLimiter:AnonSwap

platform.persistence: Records kept for a short history (about the last 16 exits)
platform.note: Reasons: REASON_LOW_MEMORY, REASON_USER_REQUESTED, REASON_EXCESSIVE_RESOURCE_USAGE, REASON_OTHER ('MemoryLimiter:AnonSwap' on 17)

capabilities.name: Expedited and user-initiated long jobs
capabilities.plain: Jobs that start soon or run long after a user action: Android expedited and UIDT, iOS 26 continued processing.
capabilities.meaning: These are the sanctioned ways to finish work the person started (upload, export). They need a visible progress surface, so apps can no longer quietly continue large jobs.

limits.headline: Can run jobs soon or for a long time after you tap something, with daily limits
limits.user_action: You tap Export, Upload or Process and the app keeps working after you leave
can: Start an expedited job that runs soon on Android
Run a long task started by you (user initiated job) on Android 14 and newer
Continue processing after you leave on iOS 26
Show progress while the job runs
cannot: Run past the daily quota for expedited jobs on Android (30 minutes at best, 5 when restricted)
Start a long job on iPhone without a foreground tap
Skip showing progress on iPhone with iOS 26
Use the GPU in the background without the Apple GPU entitlement
limits.differs: Android has daily quotas for expedited work and long jobs need a network constraint. iPhone 26 continued processing starts only from a foreground action.

story.what_it_is: Allowed ways to finish long jobs you started, like uploads or exports, with a visible progress notice.

marketing.name: User initiated data transfers
marketing.pitch: Android lets apps run long transfers you start, with a notification you can see and stop.

marketing.name: Continued processing tasks
marketing.pitch: iOS 26 lets an app keep working on a job you start, with progress shown on screen.

story.for_you: You start a big upload, a video export or a backup and then leave the app. You see a progress notice and can stop it. You are never in the dark about a long job.
story.for_makers: Makers get a proper way to finish heavy work after you leave the app. In return they must show progress. This stops apps from quietly running large jobs in the background.

use_cases.example: A video editor finishes exporting your clip after you switch apps.
A cloud app uploads a big folder and shows a progress bar in the notifications.
A game finishes downloading a large patch while you check messages.
A social app uploads a long video post after you leave.
A fitness app syncs a long workout file after the run.
A hidden kit used to run big jobs quietly, which new rules forbid.

story.android_note: Android has expedited jobs for short urgent work and user initiated transfers for long ones.
story.ios_note: iOS 26 adds continued processing for jobs you start in the app.

technical_bounds: Both need visible progress
iOS tasks are terminated first if progress is low

history.change: BGContinuedProcessingTask lets foreground started work continue with progress UI

platform.prompt_ui: Notification with progress required for UIDT
platform.persistence: Per job; stopped if the user stops it in the task manager
platform.note: Expedited quota per 24 h: Active 30 min, Working 15, Frequent 10, Rare 10, Restricted 5; UIDT has no fixed quota but needs a network constraint and notification

capabilities.name: Background start restrictions
capabilities.plain: Apps in the background cannot freely start foreground services or open screens.
capabilities.meaning: Stops hidden activity from popping up or starting long tasks while the person is elsewhere. iOS goes further: apps can only launch for a few triggers, like location or push.

fields.name: android_exemptions
fields.range: FCM high, exact alarm, visible activity

limits.headline: Can't freely start work or open screens from the background
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when an app tries to start a service or screen while hidden
can: Start a foreground service from the background only in listed exemptions on Android 12 and newer
Open a screen from the background with a special display permission or a notification tap
Wake on events on iPhone, such as push or location
cannot: Start foreground services from the background at will on Android 12 and newer
Pop up screens over other apps with no exemption
Run on iPhone with an equivalent start call; it has none
Skip tighter rules in Android 17
limits.differs: Android 12 blocks background starts and Android 17 tightens it. iPhone has no start call, only event wake ups.

story.what_it_is: The phone stops apps in the background from suddenly starting visible services or opening screens.

marketing.name: Background start restrictions
marketing.pitch: Android limits when apps in the background can start foreground services, to stop surprise activity.

story.for_you: You notice it as fewer pop ups and less hidden work. An app you are not using cannot suddenly open a screen over your game or start a long task. That keeps the phone calm.
story.for_makers: Makers must start long work from a screen you are using or a clear event, like a tap or a push. Some tricks to start hidden work are blocked. Allowed exceptions are small and listed.

use_cases.example: A game cannot throw an ad screen over your video call from the background.
A chat app starts a call screen only through a high priority message you trigger.
A navigation app starts when you tap Start, not from the background.
A workout app starts tracking after a tap or an approved trigger.
A bad app tried to pop up fake login screens from the background, which the rules stop.
A driver app uses an allowed exemption while you are on a trip.

story.android_note: Android limits when background apps can start foreground services and open screens, with a list of exceptions.
story.ios_note: iPhone goes further and lets apps wake only for a few triggers, like location or push.

technical_bounds: Exemptions are narrow and change by version

history.change: Background execution limits, no background services
FGS start from background blocked except exemptions
Background activity launch hardened for IntentSender

refs.label: Android: Restrictions on starting FGS from the background

platform.persistence: Exemptions: visible activity, high priority FCM message, exact alarm, active notification interaction, device owner
platform.note: Android 12 blocks FGS starts from background except listed exemptions; Android 17 hardens IntentSender BAL

capabilities.name: Foreground service timeouts (Android 15)
capabilities.plain: Some foreground services now stop after 6 hours in 24, and can only restart after a user returns to the app.
capabilities.meaning: A hard cap on long background syncs and media processing. It limits always-running services; Android 17 adds memory and audio limits on top.

limits.headline: Can keep some Android services running, but only about 6 hours in 24
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when an app runs a long sync or media job in the background
can: Keep a long sync or media job going for several hours at a stretch
Restart a stopped service once you open the app again
Use a short service for quick tasks, which gets about 3 minutes
cannot: Run a data sync service past the daily limit without you opening the app
Keep working after the system calls time out; the app gets only a few seconds to stop
Do this on iPhone, which has no foreground services and suspends apps as soon as work ends
limits.reach_label: Hard daily time limit on Android 15
limits.differs: Android 15 caps some long services. iPhone has no such service type and simply suspends apps when work ends.

story.what_it_is: Android now stops some always-running background tasks after about 6 hours in a day.

marketing.name: Foreground service timeouts
marketing.pitch: Android 15 puts a time limit on certain long-running background services so apps cannot drain the battery all day.

story.for_you: You never see it work. Your phone just stops apps from quietly running heavy tasks for hours, so your battery lasts longer. If an app was syncing a huge backup, it may pause until you open it again.
story.for_makers: Makers must design long jobs to finish, save progress and resume. It forces them to move big uploads and media work to smarter tools instead of one endless service.

use_cases.example: A video editor exporting a long 4K clip keeps going in the background, then must pause and resume if the export runs past the daily limit.
A running tracker that keeps a data sync service alive all day must now finish cleanly and restart when you next open it.
A big game download or patch in the background gets paused near the limit and resumes when you return to the game.
A cloud drive uploading thousands of photos overnight switches to scheduled jobs so it is not killed by the timeout.
A health app that copies sensor data from a watch all day has to batch the data instead of running nonstop.
A delivery company app that polled for new orders in the background now relies on push messages instead.

risks: Background jobs can stop mid task
Sync may lag until you reopen the app
story.android_note: Applies from Android 15. The app gets a few seconds to wrap up when the timer fires, or it crashes.
story.ios_note: iOS has no equivalent. Apps are simply put to sleep soon after their work ends.

technical_bounds: Applies to apps targeting 35 and above
Timer resets on foreground

history.change: 6 hour per 24 h timeout for dataSync and mediaProcessing (targetSdk 35)

platform.persistence: dataSync and mediaProcessing get 6 hours total per 24 h; timer resets when the app is brought to the foreground
platform.api_surface: Service.onTimeout(int, int); startForeground throws ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException when exhausted
platform.note: Service gets a few seconds after onTimeout to call stopSelf() or a RemoteServiceException is thrown; shortService limit about 3 min

capabilities.name: Foreground service types (Android 14)
capabilities.plain: Every foreground service must declare a purpose and hold the matching permission.
capabilities.meaning: Forces apps to state why they keep running (location, camera, media, phone call). The type decides which hardware and permissions the service can use, so it shows purpose to reviewers.

limits.headline: Can run long Android background tasks, but only for a declared purpose with a notification
limits.user_action: You start something long, like playing music, tracking a run, or syncing a big file
can: Keep playing audio, tracking location or syncing data while the screen is off
Show you a notification that says the work is running
Use the camera, microphone or location in the background, but only after you allowed each one
cannot: Start a background service from nowhere without a notification
Use the microphone, camera or location without their own permission
Pick any purpose it likes; Android 14 makes each service declare one type and checks it
Match this on iPhone, where background modes need an Apple approved setting instead
limits.reach_label: Ongoing, but tied to a stated purpose
limits.differs: Android uses service types with a visible notification. iPhone uses background modes set up in Xcode.

story.what_it_is: Android makes every always-running app task state its purpose, like navigation or music.

marketing.name: Foreground service types
marketing.pitch: Android 14 requires apps to declare why a service keeps running, such as media playback or location.

story.for_you: You see this as a persistent notification, such as a music player or a navigation arrow. It tells you an app is allowed to keep working while you do something else.
story.for_makers: Makers must pick the right label and get the matching permission. Google and reviewers use the label to check an app is not hiding battery heavy work behind a vague reason.

use_cases.example: A navigation app keeps turn by turn guidance running with the screen off using the location type.
A streaming app keeps playing with the phone locked using the media playback type.
A driver app keeps sharing live position during a trip while you check messages in another app.
A cycling app records your route and heart rate through the whole ride using location and health types.
A calling app keeps your microphone live during a voice call after you leave the app.
A cloud gaming or remote play app keeps its stream alive while you answer a text.

risks: Apps can misuse loose labels like special use
story.android_note: Required from Android 14. Each type needs its own permission, and camera, mic and location still need your tap.
story.ios_note: iOS uses background modes in Xcode instead, which are reviewed by Apple.

technical_bounds: Type must match actual use
Play review for sensitive types

abuse: Using a loose type like specialUse to stay alive

history.change: Foreground service type and matching permission mandatory
mediaProcessing type added; BOOT_COMPLETED receivers cannot start dataSync, camera, mediaPlayback, phoneCall, mediaProjection or microphone FGS

platform.prompt_ui: Notification required; microphone, camera, location need their own runtime grant while in use
platform.store_policy: Play: FGS type declaration form for apps targeting 34
platform.note: Types: camera, connectedDevice, dataSync, health, location, mediaPlayback, mediaProjection, microphone, phoneCall, remoteMessaging, shortService, specialUse, systemExempted; mediaProcessing added in 15

capabilities.name: Force stop and force quit
capabilities.plain: A person can kill an app: Android force stop cancels alarms; iOS force quit stops background fetch and silent push.
capabilities.meaning: Marks the clearest signal that someone does not want an app active. Both systems then block background starts until the person opens the app again.

limits.headline: Can't keep running or wake itself after you force stop (Android) or swipe it away (iPhone)
limits.user_action: You tap Force stop in Android Settings, or swipe the app up in the iPhone app switcher
can: Start working again as soon as you open the app yourself
Wake up for VoIP calls, location events or Bluetooth on iPhone, for some modes only
Keep its saved data, since force stopping does not erase anything
cannot: Receive push messages on Android until you open the app again
Fire alarms or scheduled jobs on Android after a force stop; they are cancelled
Get silent background pushes on iPhone after a force quit; Apple discards them
Run background refresh on iPhone until you open the app once more
limits.differs: Android force stop blocks pushes and cancels alarms. iPhone force quit blocks silent pushes and refresh, but some call, location and Bluetooth wakes still work.

story.what_it_is: A person can kill an app for good, and the phone then blocks it from running in the background.

marketing.name: Close an app
marketing.pitch: Apple documents how to close an app on iPhone by swiping up in the app switcher.

story.for_you: You swipe the app away or tap Force stop. From then on the app cannot send alerts or sync until you open it again, which can surprise you when a reminder never shows up.
story.for_makers: Makers treat a force stop as a clear sign someone wants out. They know push and timed jobs will fail, so they design gentle re-engagement for the next time the user returns.

use_cases.example: After you force quit a chat app, messages stop arriving as alerts until you open it.
A step counter or sleep tracker stops logging in the background and leaves a gap in your day.
A game with timed energy refills cannot send you the full energy alert after you force close it.
An ad measurement tool sees a gap in sessions and cannot record background events until the next open.
A product team sees a spike of users who force stop right after an update and treats it as a quality warning.
A banking app cannot run its background fraud checks after a force stop, so it checks again at next launch.

story.android_note: Force stop sets a stopped state that blocks broadcasts and cancels alarms and jobs.
story.ios_note: Force quit makes iOS discard silent pushes. Some wake ups like VoIP and location can still reach the app.

technical_bounds: Cannot be detected directly
Region monitoring and some modes survive force quit on iOS

history.change: Force quit prevents background fetch and silent push

platform.persistence: App stays in the stopped state until the user launches it; alarms, jobs and broadcasts cancelled; FCM not delivered
platform.note: Stopped state blocks FCM broadcasts and cancels alarms and jobs; Android 15 can also cancel on swipe for some devices

capabilities.name: iOS background modes
capabilities.plain: Xcode background modes (audio, location, VoIP, Bluetooth, fetch, push) decide what can run while closed.
capabilities.meaning: Each mode is a narrow exemption tied to a visible use. Using one for something else is an App Review rejection, so the list shows what a company claims to need.

limits.headline: Can run in the background on iPhone, but only for the kind of job Apple approved
limits.user_action: You start playback, a navigation trip, a call, or connect to a Bluetooth device
can: Keep playing audio after you leave the app, until playback ends
Keep tracking location until the app stops it, if you allowed Always
Wake up for an incoming call or a Bluetooth event
Refresh content now and then when the system decides it is a good time
cannot: Run any task it likes while closed; each mode covers one kind of job
Choose when fetch and processing happen, since iOS sets the schedule
Run in the background with no capability turned on in the app's setup
limits.reach_label: Ongoing, but only for approved jobs
limits.differs: Android has no per mode approval. It uses foreground service types and a visible notification instead.

story.what_it_is: iPhone only lets closed apps keep running for a few approved reasons, like music or navigation.

marketing.name: Background execution modes
marketing.pitch: Apple lets developers enable specific background capabilities such as audio, location, VoIP and Bluetooth in Xcode.

story.for_you: You see it as the colored bar or dot showing an app is using location or audio. It is why music keeps playing and a run keeps being recorded with the screen off.
story.for_makers: Makers must ask Apple for each mode and show a real need. The list tells reviewers what the app claims to do, and misuse can get an update rejected.

use_cases.example: A music app keeps playing with the phone locked using the audio mode.
A navigation app keeps giving turn by turn voice directions in your pocket.
A workout app records a bike ride route and heart rate while the screen is off.
A calling app wakes the phone for an incoming call using the VoIP mode.
A home app stays in touch with a Bluetooth lock so it can unlock as you arrive.
A multiplayer game uses the audio mode for in game voice chat that keeps going when you switch apps.

risks: Some apps stretch a mode to stay alive
Hard to tell which apps run in the background
story.android_note: Android uses foreground service types instead of one entitlement per mode.
story.ios_note: Each mode has its own run window, such as until music ends or until location is stopped.

technical_bounds: Review rejects misuse

abuse: Abusing audio or location for keep-alive

history.change: VoIP pushes must show a CallKit call

platform.store_policy: Play: FGS type declaration
platform.api_surface: Foreground service types as the closest analog
platform.note: Android uses FGS types instead of per-mode entitlements

capabilities.name: iOS app refresh and processing tasks
capabilities.plain: iOS lets apps request short refreshes (about 30 s) or longer idle processing; timing is up to the system.
capabilities.meaning: The only system scheduled background work on iOS. Timing follows how often the person uses the app; dormant installs may never run.

limits.headline: Can ask iPhone for short refreshes of about 30 seconds, but the system picks the time
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when iOS decides to wake the app, often after you use it a lot
can: Refresh content for about 30 seconds so it is fresh when you open the app
Run longer jobs, like cleanup or a sync, for a few minutes when the phone is idle and charging
Schedule up to about 10 pending requests
cannot: Choose the exact time; iOS can delay or skip a request
Run longer jobs while you are using the phone on battery
Repeat faster than every 15 minutes on Android, where that is the minimum
limits.reach_label: Short bursts, timed by the system
limits.differs: Android periodic work repeats at most every 15 minutes. iPhone gives no guaranteed interval.

story.what_it_is: iPhone lets apps ask for short refreshes or longer idle jobs, but the system picks the timing.

marketing.name: Background Tasks
marketing.pitch: Apple describes BGTaskScheduler as the way to refresh content and run longer jobs when the system judges it a good time.

story.for_you: You never see it. Your news or email app has fresh content when you open it because iOS ran a short refresh earlier. If you rarely open an app, it may never get a turn.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to prefetch content and sync data so the app feels instant. They cannot control the timing, so they pair it with push messages for urgent updates.

use_cases.example: A news app downloads the morning headlines in a short refresh so the front page is ready when you wake.
A podcast app fetches new episodes while your phone charges overnight in a longer processing task.
A notes app syncs your edits to the cloud in the background so another device is up to date.
A store app refreshes your order status so the screen is already current when you open it.
A health app processes a day of sensor data while you sleep and charge your phone.
An ad and measurement tool uses the short window to upload queued events from the day.

risks: Can be used to poll for signals
story.android_note: Android periodic work has a 15 minute minimum interval.
story.ios_note: App refresh is about 30 seconds. Idle processing runs for minutes when charging.

technical_bounds: No guaranteed timing
Not run after force quit

platform.note: Android periodic work min interval 15 min

capabilities.name: Low Power Mode, Battery Saver and Background App Refresh state
capabilities.plain: Apps can see whether the phone is in a power saving state and adapt, and iOS shows if background refresh is on.
capabilities.meaning: Reveals whether the person is low on battery or has background activity disabled. Apps use it to defer work; it also hints at device habits.

limits.headline: Can see if your phone is saving power, and slow itself down to match
limits.user_action: Nothing. The app checks this when it opens or before it starts background work
can: Tell if Low Power Mode or Battery Saver is on
Check on iPhone whether Background App Refresh is available, restricted or turned off
Pause syncing, animations or downloads to save battery
cannot: Turn Low Power Mode or Battery Saver on or off for you
Force background work to continue when the system has paused it
Change your Background App Refresh setting
limits.reach_label: A simple on or off check
limits.differs: iPhone Low Power Mode pauses background fetch and mail fetch. Android Battery Saver restricts background activity, location and sync.

story.what_it_is: Apps can tell if your phone is saving power, and iPhone shows if background refresh is on.

marketing.name: Low Power Mode
marketing.pitch: Apple pitches Low Power Mode as a way to stretch battery by reducing background activity and some visual effects.

marketing.name: Battery Saver
marketing.pitch: Google describes Battery Saver as a mode that extends battery life by limiting background activity.

story.for_you: You never see apps read it. But when your battery is low, games look a little plainer and apps stop syncing, because they noticed you switched on power saving.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to be kind to the battery, such as lowering frame rate or delaying uploads. Others can read it as a hint about habits, like someone who is often low on charge.

use_cases.example: A racing game drops from 60 to 30 frames per second when it sees Low Power Mode, so you can keep playing longer.
A streaming app picks a lower video quality and stops downloading ahead when battery saving is on.
A navigation app dims the map animation but keeps directions going.
An ad network sees many low battery devices and avoids heavy video ads that would drain them.
A product team splits crash and speed reports by power mode to find problems only seen when saving power.
A fraud tool notes whether the device state looks normal for the account holder.

story.android_note: Battery Saver limits background work, location and sync.
story.ios_note: Low Power Mode pauses background fetch and mail. Apps can also see if Background App Refresh is on, off or limited.

technical_bounds: Both are readable with no prompt

history.change: Low Power Mode and isLowPowerModeEnabled introduced

platform.note: Battery Saver restricts background activity, location and sync

capabilities.name: OEM background killers
capabilities.plain: Many Android makers add extra killers that stop apps beyond what Google's rules allow.
capabilities.meaning: Explains why push and alarms fail on some phones: aggressive task killers, autostart lists and battery managers. Developers ask users to whitelist; no API can force it.

limits.headline: Can't count on running in the background on some Android phones, since brands add extra killers
limits.user_action: Nothing. The phone's maker stops the app on its own after you leave it
can: Run normally while you have the app open
Ask you to switch on autostart or remove battery limits in the phone's own settings
Keep working in the background if you turn off the maker's limits for it
cannot: Check from inside the app whether the maker's killer is on; there is no common way
Turn off the maker's battery limits by itself
Behave the same on every Android phone; each brand differs
Face this on iPhone, which has one background rule for everyone
limits.differs: Many Android brands stop apps beyond Google's rules. iPhone has a single consistent background policy.

story.what_it_is: Some Android phone makers add extra app killers that stop apps beyond Google's rules.
story.for_you: You may miss alarms, chat alerts or fitness tracking on some brands, even with every setting on. You may be told to dig through battery menus and allow the app to autostart.
story.for_makers: Makers lose reliable alerts and reminders on these phones and cannot detect or fix it with code. They write help pages and in app guides that ask people to whitelist the app.

use_cases.example: A chat app on some phones stops delivering message alerts after the screen is off, so the app shows a guide to turn off the battery manager.
A medication reminder app fails to ring at night because the phone maker killed it, so it asks to be put on a protected list.
A run tracker on certain phones stops recording mid run, so the app links to a help page for that brand.
A security camera app misses a motion alert because the phone maker shut the app down.
A game that sends a timer alert for a finished build gets silenced, so players miss the reminder.
Developers check a public list of phone brands to see which ones kill apps and adjust their guide.

risks: Hard for apps to detect or fix
story.android_note: This is Android only. It depends on the phone brand and has no standard way to check.
story.ios_note: iOS has one background policy for every iPhone, so this problem does not exist.

technical_bounds: No API; vendor specific
Google CTS does not cover vendor killers

history.change: Doze gave vendors a template; vendor killers grew after

refs.label: Android: Optimize for Doze and App Standby

platform.prompt_ui: Vendor specific settings: autostart, protected apps, battery manager
platform.store_policy: Play: battery opt-out prompts limited
platform.api_surface: dontkillmyapp.com lists vendors (Xiaomi, Huawei, Oppo, Vivo, Samsung and others)
platform.note: Behavior varies by vendor; no portable detection

capabilities.name: Region monitoring and geofences
capabilities.plain: Wakes the app when the device enters or leaves a circle: 20 regions on iOS, 100 geofences on Android.
capabilities.meaning: Lets a retailer know when someone arrives at a store or leaves home. The caps force apps to rotate regions, and the OS keeps them even after the app is closed.

limits.headline: Can wake the app when you enter or leave set places, up to 20 on iPhone
limits.user_action: You turn on place reminders, home arrival alerts, or a store offer feature, and allow Always location
can: Wake the app when you cross into or out of a circle it set
Send you a reminder when you arrive or leave, even with the app closed
Watch up to 20 places on iPhone, or 100 on Android
cannot: Watch more places than the limit allows
Know your exact route; it only learns that you crossed an edge
Do this without Always location on Android or iPhone
React instantly; Android can take about 2 to 3 minutes, and small circles are less precise
limits.reach_label: Ongoing, but only for set places
limits.differs: iPhone allows 20 regions and may need a device unlock after reboot. Android allows 100 geofences, with a 2 to 3 minute average delay.

story.what_it_is: The phone can wake an app when you enter or leave a map circle, even if the app is closed.

marketing.name: Region monitoring
marketing.pitch: Apple lets apps watch circular areas and be told when you cross them, to power place based features.

marketing.name: Geofencing
marketing.pitch: Google pitches geofencing as a way to react when a device enters or exits an area around a place.

story.for_makers: Emulators let fraudsters run hundreds of fake users. Makers check build fields and hardware to block bots, fake installs and cheaters. Real phones with odd settings can get flagged by mistake.

story.for_makers: Matching the stock camera's processing makes third party apps feel premium. Camera permission is still needed, and the extras mainly improve image quality, not access.

use_cases.example: You take a night photo in Instagram and it looks bright and sharp.
A pro camera app uses the phone's portrait blur on a headshot.
A video call app uses HDR to fix a dark room.
A marketplace app shows clearer item photos at night.

An AR game gets a cleaner image under low light.

marketing.name: Google Cast

story.for_makers: Makers use it for second screens like game controls on the phone and the game on the TV, slide decks and video players. It is mostly a layout feature.

A streaming app plays a movie on your TV while your phone becomes the remote.
A slide app shows slides on a projector and notes on your phone.
A drawing app shows a large clean canvas on a monitor while tools stay on the tablet.
A car display app shows maps on the dashboard screen and a list on your phone.
A sports app shows a live game on the TV and a stat feed on your phone.
A sales app presents a customer demo on a conference room screen.

marketing.name: LiDAR Scanner
marketing.pitch: Measure the distance to objects and map rooms in 3D for AR, photography and measuring.

story.for_you: A measuring app instantly tells you how tall a door is, or a room scanner builds a 3D model as you walk around it. Nothing seems to be recorded, but your room shape is captured.
story.for_makers: Depth makes AR objects hide behind real furniture, makes portrait mode sharp, and lets apps build 3D models of homes and bodies. Face depth data is sensitive because it can describe a face shape, so access is tightly limited.

use_cases.example: A virtual ball bounces off your real sofa and rolls behind your table.
A home improvement app scans your room so it can suggest furniture that fits.
A 3D scan app builds a model of a statue or a sneaker for sharing.
An AR game hides virtual enemies behind walls and corners in your real room.
A face unlock flow uses a depth map of the face, not just a photo, so a picture cannot fool it.
A measuring app finds the width of a window.
A fitness app counts reps by tracking the body in 3D.

marketing.pitch: Let your app act as a contactless card, such as a payment or transit card, without special hardware.

An office badge app opens doors when you tap your phone.
A bank app sends a one time code to the shop's reader.
A car sharing app taps the car to unlock.

limits.headline: Can use the phone's secure chip only with special approval

can: Store keys, badges and payment credentials on the secure chip
Let banks, car makers and employers issue keys without Apple or Google Wallet
Run on iPhone in selected countries and the EEA
cannot: Use the chip on iPhone without Apple's entitlement, agreement and fee
Use the chip on Android without the chip vendor's access rules

story.what_it_is: Lets an approved app store and run keys, badges and payment cards inside the phone's tamper proof chip.

marketing.name: NFC and SE Platform
marketing.pitch: Approved apps can use the phone's secure element for tap payments, car keys, IDs and more.

story.for_you: You tap your phone on a hotel door, a car or a payment reader and it works as fast as a card. The key is held in a locked chip, so someone who copies your app cannot copy the key.
story.for_makers: The chip is the safest place on a phone for car keys, bank cards and access badges. Banks, car makers and employers want to use it for their own brand. Platforms limit it to vetted companies and regions.

use_cases.example: A car maker's app opens and starts the car from the phone's secure chip.
A hotel app issues a room key valid for exactly your stay.
An employer's app holds a badge for the office door and the parking gate.
A student ID opens dorms and pays at the cafeteria.
A bank puts its own card in its app and takes taps without the system wallet.
A government app holds a digital ID checked by tapping a reader.
A home lock holds a house key and shares it with family.

story.android_note: Most Android apps use software card emulation. Third party secure chip access needs rules set by the chip owner.

story.for_makers: USB turns the phone into a tool for pros. A creator can plug in an audio interface or camera, and engineers can program boards. Android opens raw access to apps. iPhone keeps raw access for iPad.

A streamer plugs in a USB camera and microphone and goes live from a phone.
A hobbyist programs a microcontroller board straight from a phone.
A gamer plugs a wired controller into a phone for console style play on the go.
A technician connects a medical or lab sensor and logs readings.
A shop plugs in a barcode scanner or card reader for the till.

marketing.name: Wear OS
marketing.pitch: Wear OS is Google's watch platform, with apps that can sync with Android phones.

story.for_you: You see messages, workouts or maps on your wrist and tap a reply. Behind the scenes your health numbers, location and notifications move between the watch and phone.
story.for_makers: A watch app keeps people glancing at the brand all day. It collects steady health and activity data and can send alerts. The link between the watch and phone often carries more than the person sees.

use_cases.example: A running app shows your pace on the wrist and saves the route to your phone when you finish.
A diabetes app shows your glucose level on the watch face and warns you before a drop.
A map app buzzes your wrist for each turn so you do not look at the phone.
A music app lets you control playback on the phone from the watch.
A chat app lets you read and reply by voice on the wrist.
A home app lets you unlock the door or turn on lights from the watch.
A wallet app taps to pay with the watch when your phone is in a bag.

story.for_makers: Without the line, the advertising ID returns zeros. It cuts ad tracking in apps that skip the declaration and signals to Play reviewers that an app uses ads.

A kids app leaves it out on purpose, so the ID is always zeros.
A retailer declares it so install attribution works.
An ad SDK checks for the permission and falls back to contextual ads.
Play checks the manifest and the Data safety form for matching claims.
A developer finds the ID suddenly returns zeros after updating the target version.

story.ios_note: iOS uses the ATT prompt instead.

marketing.pitch: Apple's service that lets a server check that requests come from a legitimate instance of its app on Apple hardware.

story.for_you: You do not see it. Behind the scenes your phone makes a secret key for the app and signs important requests. The result is fewer bots and fake copies of the app, and more accounts that just work.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to stop cloned apps, scripted bots and tampered builds from hitting their servers. It protects revenue in games and shops, and keeps free offers from being farmed. The cost is that jailbroken phones may be refused.

use_cases.example: A multiplayer game checks that a score comes from the real app, not a cheat tool, before it goes on a leaderboard.

marketing.pitch: Passwords, cards and codes appear above the keyboard so you can fill a form with one tap.

marketing.pitch: Android fills in saved passwords, addresses and payment details across apps from one place.

story.for_you: You tap a login box and your saved username and password pop up above the keyboard. One tap fills it. You skip typing and avoid weak passwords.
story.for_makers: Makers want sign up and checkout to be fast, because every extra typed field loses buyers. The password manager in the middle sees which fields an app shows, so its trust level matters.

use_cases.example: At checkout you tap the card box and your saved card and address fill in, so you buy before you change your mind.
An Uber login screen fills your email and password with one tap on a new phone.
A food delivery app fills your home address and phone so a hungry order takes seconds.
A bank app fills a saved username while keeping the password behind a Face ID check.
A game store login fills your account details so you can start playing after a reinstall.
An attacker shows a fake login box in the hope the autofill service fills it, which is why good managers check the app identity first.

story.android_note: Android lets you pick any autofill service, and older ones could read the whole screen layout.
story.ios_note: iPhone autofill is built into the keyboard and password manager, and apps only see what you choose to fill.

technical_bounds: Secure fields can be blocked from autofill by developers

history.change: Password AutoFill and one time code fill

platform.prompt_ui: User must pick the Autofill service in Settings
platform.note: Android 14 pushes passkeys and passwords through Credential Manager as well.

capabilities.name: Credential provider role (third party password and passkey manager)
capabilities.plain: An app registers as the person's password and passkey manager for the whole system.
capabilities.meaning: The chosen manager can supply logins for every other app and site, and sees which services the person signs into. It is one of the most trusted roles on the phone.

limits.headline: Can act as your phone's password and passkey manager once you turn it on
limits.user_action: You open Settings and choose this app as your passwords and passkeys provider
can: Save passwords and passkeys that other apps and sites ask to store
Offer matching logins when you sign in to another app or website
Unlock a login after checking your fingerprint, face or master password
Offer passkeys to other apps and sites on iPhone from iOS 17
cannot: Become your provider until you turn it on in Settings
See logins stored by other providers
Hand over a login without your approval on screen
Work in apps that block autofill
limits.reach_label: Every login you store with it
limits.differs: Android has a system role and a default provider choice. iPhone has an Autofill provider switch and added passkey support in iOS 17.

story.what_it_is: An app becomes your phone's main place for passwords and passkeys.

marketing.name: Credential Manager providers
marketing.pitch: Android lets password managers plug in so you can sign in with passkeys and passwords from your chosen app.

marketing.name: Passwords and passkeys providers
marketing.pitch: Apple lets other password apps supply logins and passkeys system wide, alongside its own Passwords app.

story.for_you: You pick a manager in Settings and from then on it offers your logins in every app and website. You also see its name at sign in. It feels like one safe place for all your accounts.
story.for_makers: For a password manager this role is the product: it is how its logins show up everywhere without copy and paste. It is also the most trusted job on a phone, because it can see which services you use.

use_cases.example: A password app fills your work login in a banking app, a news app and a browser, all from one unlock.
A manager shows you only the passkey for the real site and warns you that a look alike site has none saved.
You sign back into a game on a new phone and your manager fills the login and the one time code in a single step.
A company rolls out one approved manager to staff phones so every work app signs in the same way.
A family plan lets a parent share one safe login with a child's phone without typing the password in front of them.
Your bank app asks to create a passkey, and your chosen manager stores it and syncs it to your tablet.

story.android_note: Android treats this as a switch in Settings, and you can have more than one provider with one set as the main.
story.ios_note: iPhone lets third party managers act as the system provider, and the user turns them on in Settings under Passwords.

technical_bounds: User chooses provider explicitly in Settings on both OS

history.change: Password manager extensions as AutoFill providers

platform.prompt_ui: User picks provider in Settings > Passwords & accounts
platform.store_policy: Play: credential manager apps follow User Data policy
platform.note: Provider apps must be enabled by the user; Android 15 adds default-provider behaviors.

capabilities.name: DeviceCheck two bits
capabilities.plain: Apple stores two bits per device per developer on its servers.
capabilities.meaning: Lets a developer mark a device (for example, trial used) with 2 bits that persist across reinstall and device wipe; no other data.

limits.headline: Can store two yes or no flags about your device on Apple's servers
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the app's server asks Apple about your device
can: Set or look up 2 bits on Apple's servers for this device and this developer
Remember a device was flagged (for example, a used free trial) even after you reinstall
Learn the month the bits were last changed
cannot: Store anything beyond 2 bits and a date
Share the bits with other developers
See your Apple ID, name or any personal detail
Work on Android; there is no equivalent
limits.differs: Only iPhone has DeviceCheck. Android gives integrity verdicts but no storage.

story.what_it_is: Apple lets an app store two private yes or no flags about your phone on its servers.

marketing.name: DeviceCheck
marketing.pitch: Apple offers two bits per device so developers can remember simple things like a used free trial.

story.for_you: You never see it. It can mean that if you used a free trial once, the app may still know after you delete it and reinstall. You cannot clear it yourself.
story.for_makers: Makers use these two bits to stop people from claiming a free trial again and again, or to mark a phone that abused a promo. It survives reinstall and even a wipe of the device, which is why it works so well for abuse control.

use_cases.example: A music streaming app marks your phone when you finish a free trial so a new email cannot get another one.
A mobile game flags a phone that abused a gift code so the same phone cannot claim it again on a new account.
A dating app remembers that a phone was banned for harassment, so a fresh profile does not slip through.
A store limits a welcome coupon to one claim per phone even after an app reinstall.
An ad network flags a device that produced fake installs, then discounts its traffic.
A bank app marks a phone used in a known scam so later sign ins from it get extra checks.

story.android_note: Android has no exact twin. Developers use Play Integrity and server side checks instead.
story.ios_note: This is Apple only. Each developer gets its own two bits per device, so it cannot link different developers.

technical_bounds: Server only
2 bits max

platform.note: Play Integrity gives verdicts, not storage

capabilities.plain: Asks the phone's wallet for a verified age, name or license, with the person's consent.
capabilities.meaning: Shares only chosen attributes (age over 21, name, address) cryptographically signed by an issuer. Replaces ID photos and upload flows when it works.

limits.user_action: You tap Verify my age or Verify my ID and approve the wallet prompt
can: Ask the wallet for a specific item, such as over 21, your name, or your license
Receive a signed answer after you approve in the wallet
Use the proof to unlock an age gated or ID gated action
Accept the proof on a web page through the browser
cannot: Receive anything you decline on the wallet screen
See credentials you never added to a wallet
Skip the approval prompt
Keep asking for new proofs without a new prompt each time
limits.differs: Android works through Credential Manager and registered wallets. iPhone needs an Apple entitlement and uses Verify with Wallet.

story.what_it_is: An app asks your wallet to prove one fact about you, like your age, instead of uploading an ID photo.

marketing.name: Digital Credentials API
marketing.pitch: Android lets apps and sites request verified details from a wallet, with a clear consent screen.

marketing.name: Verify with Wallet
marketing.pitch: Apple lets apps ask for age or ID details from Wallet and shows what is being shared first.

story.for_you: You see a sheet that says which facts the app wants, like 'over 21' or your name. You approve with Face ID or a fingerprint and nothing else is shared. No photo of your license is needed.
story.for_makers: Makers get a signed fact from the government issuer, so there is less fraud and less ID data stored to protect. It cuts drop offs from long upload steps. They must request only the facts they need, or regulators and users push back.

use_cases.example: An online liquor store asks if you are over 21 and your wallet answers yes without showing your birth date.
A hotel app lets you share your name and ID for check in before you arrive, so you skip the desk.
A bank opens an account in minutes by taking verified name and address from your wallet.
A game with mature content checks your age band once instead of trusting a checkbox.
A social site proves a new user is an adult before it shows age limited rooms.
A car rental or ride app confirms a valid license from your wallet before it unlocks a car.

story.android_note: Android shows a system picker that lists the wallets that can answer the request.
story.ios_note: iPhone shows its own sheet with the exact attributes and requires Face ID, with state support rolling out slowly.

technical_bounds: Verifier must be vetted; credentials issued by supported states and countries only

history.change: Verify with Wallet in apps and web

capabilities.name: Firebase installation ID
capabilities.plain: A random per-install ID created by the Firebase SDK.
capabilities.meaning: Fresh per app install; many SDKs use it as a first-party ID and link it to other IDs server-side.

limits.headline: Can recognize this one install of the app with a random ID, until it is removed
limits.user_action: Nothing. The ID is created the first time the app connects to the internet
can: Tell one install of the app apart from another with a 22 character random ID
Link usage, crashes and messages to that same install over time
Keep the same ID until you clear the app's data or uninstall it
cannot: Follow you to other apps or other phones; the ID belongs to this install only
Survive an uninstall or Clear data; a new ID is made afterward
Stay alive forever on Android if the app goes unused; it is deleted after 270 days

story.what_it_is: A random ID made for each app install by Google's Firebase toolkit.

marketing.name: Firebase installations
marketing.pitch: Developer pitch: a stable, unique ID for each install of your app, used by Firebase services like messaging and analytics.

story.for_you: You never see it. It quietly lets the app and Google's tools tell your phone apart from every other install, and it resets if you delete and reinstall the app.
story.for_makers: Makers get a free, always available ID to count users, send push notifications and run tests. It lets crash reports, experiments and notifications line up for one install without asking for any permission.

use_cases.example: A game studio uses the install ID to give one phone the same A/B test version of the tutorial every time it opens the game.
A chat app uses the ID as the address for push notifications, so a message reaches the right phone.
A product team counts daily active installs and links crash reports to one install without asking you to sign in.
An ad network links an install to a later in-app purchase so it can tell which campaign paid off.
A store app shows you the same test version of its checkout page on each visit, so results stay clean.
A bank sees ten new accounts opened from one install ID and flags a possible fraud ring.

risks: Can be joined to other IDs on a server
story.android_note: Available to any app that includes Firebase, with no prompt.
story.ios_note: Works the same way on iPhone, created fresh for each install of the app.

technical_bounds: Per-app, not cross-app

refs.label: Android: Best practices for unique identifiers

platform.store_policy: Play: data safety disclosure
platform.note: 22-character ID, valid until app data is cleared or the app is uninstalled; deleted if unused for 270 days

Show your player name and profile picture in the game

Post scores and unlock achievements

story.what_it_is: You sign into the phone's built in game account, so scores, saves and friends follow you.

marketing.name: Google Play Games services
marketing.pitch: One game profile that carries your achievements, cloud saves and leaderboards across devices.

marketing.name: Game Center
marketing.pitch: Apple's social gaming network for friends, leaderboards and achievements across your Apple devices.

story.for_you: When you open a game you see a small welcome banner with your gamer name. Your progress is saved to the account and shows up on a new phone. Friends can see your scores and invite you to play.
story.for_makers: Makers get a ready made player ID, friends list, leaderboard and cloud save without building their own. It also gives the platform a link between your play in many games, which helps with recommendations and retention.

use_cases.example: A puzzle game restores your levels and coins on a new phone after you sign in with your game account.
A racing game shows your lap time against friends on a leaderboard.
A multiplayer game uses your friends list to start a match or invite someone straight into your party.
An AR title saves your collection to the game account so a lost phone does not wipe it.
A kids game uses an account managed by a parent so achievements are saved without a new password.
A studio sees returning players across devices and counts a person once, not three phones.

story.android_note: Android uses Play Games, and it signs in automatically when the player has a Google account on the phone.
story.ios_note: iPhone uses Game Center, and the player signs in once in Settings and can turn it off per app.

technical_bounds: Friends list needs player consent

capabilities.name: Hardware backed keys (Keystore and Secure Enclave)
capabilities.plain: Creates cryptographic keys that never leave the phone's secure chip.
capabilities.meaning: A device-bound key proves that a request comes from one specific phone. The iOS Keychain can survive app deletion, which lets services recognise a returning device.

limits.headline: Can make secret keys that stay locked inside your phone's security chip
limits.user_action: Nothing, or you confirm with fingerprint or face when the app sets up secure sign in
can: Create a key in the phone's secure chip
Sign data or log in with that key without exposing it
Require your fingerprint or face each time the key is used
Prove which phone model and security patch level it is on (Android)
cannot: Take the key out of the chip or copy it to a server
Use the key after you remove the screen lock, when set to require one
Use other key types in the iPhone Secure Enclave; it only supports P-256
Move the key to a new phone
limits.reach_label: Keys only usable on this phone
limits.differs: Android can prove the model and patch level. iPhone Secure Enclave keys are limited to one key type and are checked by Face ID or Touch ID.

story.what_it_is: An app makes a secret key that is stored in a locked chip and never leaves your phone.

marketing.name: Android Keystore
marketing.pitch: Keys live in protected hardware so even malware cannot copy them out of the phone.

marketing.name: Secure Enclave
marketing.pitch: A separate chip that holds keys and checks Face ID or Touch ID without sharing them with the app.

story.for_you: You never see the key. What you notice is smooth, safe actions like approving a payment with a face scan, and a login that does not need a password. The secret stays on the phone.
story.for_makers: Makers can prove that a login or payment came from one specific phone, which is strong protection against stolen passwords. The key can also tie an account to a device, and on iPhone some keychain items survive an uninstall, which helps services recognize a returning phone.

use_cases.example: A bank signs each money transfer with a hardware key so a stolen password alone cannot move funds.
A wallet app approves a tap to pay with a key that only unlocks after you scan your face.
A game uses a device key to sign purchase requests and block fake receipts.
A company ties staff logins to company phones with keys, so a copied password is useless on another device.
A cryptocurrency app keeps its signing key inside the chip so malware cannot read it.
A digital car key stores a key in the chip so your phone can unlock and start the car.

story.android_note: Android may keep keys in the main secure chip or a separate StrongBox chip, depending on the phone model.
story.ios_note: iPhone keychain items can survive deleting an app, so a service may still recognise a returning phone.

technical_bounds: Key material is never extractable

capabilities.plain: A per-vendor iOS ID that is the same across one developer's apps.
capabilities.meaning: Lets a developer link their own apps on one phone with no prompt. Resets when the last app by that vendor is deleted.

limits.headline: Can recognize you across apps from the same developer on iPhone, but not other developers
limits.user_action: Nothing. Any app can ask for it as soon as it opens
can: Use one shared ID across all of one developer's apps on your iPhone
Count how many different people use the developer's apps
Keep the same ID until every app from that developer is deleted
cannot: Match you to apps from other developers; each developer gets a different ID
Exist on Android; there is no direct match, only Android ID
Stay the same after you delete all of that developer's apps
Be available before your first unlock after a restart

story.what_it_is: An iOS ID that is the same for all apps from one developer on your phone.

marketing.name: identifierForVendor
marketing.pitch: Developer pitch: an alphanumeric string that identifies the device to the app's vendor, shared by that vendor's apps.

story.for_you: You never see it and no pop up appears. It lets one company, like a game studio with several games, know the same phone runs all its apps. It resets when you delete the last app from that company.
story.for_makers: Makers can link their own apps on one phone with no prompt and without Apple's tracking rules. It helps with saving progress, fraud checks and cross promotion between their own titles.

use_cases.example: A studio that makes five puzzle games sees that the same phone plays all of them and offers a bonus in the new game.
A streaming company uses it to hide its trial offer from a phone that already used it in a sister app.
A publisher builds an audience of people who play several of its own apps and sells ads to that group.
A developer joins crash logs from three of its apps to see that one phone is failing everywhere.
A bank app group spots many accounts that share one vendor ID and applies stricter checks.
A retailer with a store app and a coupon app knows both are on the same phone and syncs your points.

story.android_note: Android has no matching ID, so this does not exist there.
story.ios_note: Free to read with no prompt and it is not limited by the Ask App Not to Track choice because it stays inside one company.

technical_bounds: Scoped to one vendor

can: Create a passkey for your account tied to the app and its website
Sign you in with a passkey instead of a password
Show a system sheet listing the passkeys you already have
Sync passkeys through your password manager or cloud keychain
cannot: See your private passkey or your screen lock
Use a passkey without your approval each time
Use the passkey on a different website or app than it was made for
Work on very old phones without Google Play services (Android)
