limits.differs: Android uses Credential Manager. iPhone needs the app tied to its website and supports other managers from iOS 17.

story.what_it_is: You sign in with a face or fingerprint scan instead of a password.

marketing.name: Passkeys
marketing.pitch: Sign in with Face ID or Touch ID instead of passwords, and passkeys sync across your Apple devices.

marketing.name: Passkeys
marketing.pitch: Android and Google make passkeys the simple, safer way to sign in without remembering passwords.

story.for_you: You tap sign in, glance at your phone or touch the sensor, and you are in. No password to remember or type. A fake site cannot steal it because the passkey only works on the real one.
story.for_makers: Makers see fewer password resets, fewer stolen accounts and quicker sign ups. It also moves the key storage to Apple or Google, so recovery and lock in become the platform's problem and power.

use_cases.example: A shop lets you create a passkey after your first order, then logs you in next time with a face scan.
A bank swaps password and text code for a passkey, which cuts phishing losses.
A game platform signs you in with a passkey so a hacked reused password cannot steal your skins.
A social app lets you sign in with a passkey from your tablet through the shared keychain.
An airline app signs you in with a passkey, so you check in fast at the airport.
A company login uses passkeys so staff stop falling for fake login pages.

marketing.name: Play Integrity API
marketing.pitch: Google helps apps detect risky or fake devices and apps so they can fight fraud, cheating and abuse.

story.for_you: You never see it. It runs in the background when you log in, buy something or play online. It can make a game or bank app refuse to run on a rooted phone or a custom system.
story.for_makers: Makers get a signed answer from Google about whether the device is real, the app is untouched and it was installed from Google Play. They use it to cut cheaters, bots and card fraud. It also locks out some honest users with custom software.

A bank app refuses to open on a rooted phone, because malware could read the screen.
A payments app verifies the device before it approves a high value transfer.
A sale app limits scripted bots grabbing limited stock by checking each request.
A streaming app uses it to block pirated, repackaged copies of the app.
A new sign up is checked for emulators so one person cannot create thousands of fake accounts.

A product team counts unique devices over months without asking for a login.
A company device manager uses it to know which phone is which in its fleet.

A shopping app remembers a coupon was used on this phone even after you reinstall.
A wallet app notices a reinstall by the same person and avoids sending a second verification text.
A dating or banking app spots a banned user who deleted the app and started again.
A streaming app limits a free trial to one per phone, even if you remove and add the app.
An ad firm keeps a stable ID that outlives uninstall so campaign results are not broken by reinstalls.

story.ios_note: Keychain items often remain after the app is deleted, and the person cannot easily see or clear them.

A bank confirms who you are when you open a new account from your couch.
A car rental desk lets you skip the counter by sharing your license from your wallet.

A building uses wallet IDs to sign in guests without paper badges.

story.for_you: You never see it. It works behind the scenes so a protected movie will play, and it may also act as a long lasting tag on your phone that survives clearing app data.
story.for_makers: Streaming services need it to give out licences and set quality levels. Because it can stay the same after a reset, some apps use it as a hard to remove device ID for fraud checks and device tracking.

use_cases.example: A streaming app checks your phone's Widevine level before allowing HD or 4K playback.
A service limits how many phones one account can download offline shows to, counting them by device ID.
A fraud team blocks an account sharing scam that signs in from the same hardware over and over.
A cloud gaming app checks that a phone has secure video decoding before it allows protected streams.
A tracker reads a value that outlives a reset to rebuild a profile after you clear your ad ID.
A live sports app uses DRM licences so a match feed cannot be recorded by ripping the stream.

marketing.pitch: Apps can ask for an age range that a parent or user has shared, without learning exact birth dates.

marketing.name: Play Age Signals
marketing.pitch: Google gives apps an age signal to help them follow child safety laws.

story.for_you: You or a parent set your age once. An app may ask for your age group, and you may see a prompt asking whether to share it. Teens may see a more limited version of the app.
story.for_makers: New laws push app makers to protect children, and a trustworthy age signal is easier than checking IDs. The rule is that the app gets a band like 13 to 15, not a date. Getting it wrong either shuts out young users or puts them in unsafe spaces.

use_cases.example: A social app switches off direct messages from strangers for people in the teen band.
A game turns off open voice chat and loot box offers for under 13 players.
A video app picks a kids profile when the age signal says a child is watching.
A dating app keeps minors out by asking the phone for an age check instead of a typed birthday.
A store hides age restricted items from younger shoppers.
A learning app asks a parent to approve a child's account when the age band says under 13.

marketing.pitch: Google tells servers whether a device, app and account look real or risky.

story.for_you: You do not see it. It sits behind a sign up, a purchase or a score upload and quietly says 'this looks real'. If your phone is jailbroken or rooted, an app may stop working.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to block bots, cheats and cloned apps. It is a device level proof, not a person level ID, which helps with privacy. It still decides which phones are allowed and which are turned away.

use_cases.example: A game server checks that a match result came from the real game, not a modified copy.
A bank checks that a transfer request came from its real app before it moves any money.
A ticket seller blocks scripts that buy up concert seats by checking each purchase.
A social app slows fake account creation by asking new devices to prove they are real.
An ad platform removes fake installs by confirming the app and device were genuine.
An AI app protects its paid server by only answering the true app.

story.for_makers: Makers use it to show the right input screen. Ad and fraud tools also treat the keyboard list as a fingerprint, since a third party keyboard or a second language makes you stand out. It also hints at origin and language skills.

use_cases.example: A chat app shows a right to left layout when you add an Arabic or Hebrew keyboard.
A language app notices you have a Japanese keyboard and offers kana practice.
A social app suggests posts in your second language.
A keyboard app checks if it is enabled so it can show a setup guide.
An ad company infers that you are bilingual or an expat from the keyboard list.
A fraud tool compares keyboards with the account's claimed country to catch fake sign ups.

story.android_note: Android apps can list enabled input methods with few limits.
story.ios_note: iPhone apps can read this only with an approved Apple reason, and the list is meant to stay on device.

technical_bounds: iOS keyboard info needs a declared reason

limits.headline: Can see and tap other apps' screens on Android, once you turn it on
limits.user_action: You open Settings, then Accessibility, pick the app and accept the full control warning
can: See text on the screen of any app
Tap, swipe and type in other apps
Do actions like Back and Home for you
cannot: Turn itself on; you must switch it on in Settings
Be enabled in a sideloaded app on Android 13 and later until you allow restricted settings
See sensitive fields on Android 17 unless it is a real accessibility tool
Control other apps on iPhone
limits.differs: Android lets an enabled service see and control any app; iPhone has no matching cross app control.

story.what_it_is: A powerful Android tool that lets an app read other apps' screens and tap on your behalf.

marketing.name: Accessibility services
marketing.pitch: Build tools that help people with disabilities use their phone, by reading screens and acting for them.

story.for_you: A special settings screen asks you to turn it on, with a scary warning. Once on, a helper can read what is on the screen and tap for you. A screen reader speaks every button aloud.
story.for_makers: Screen readers and switch tools could not exist without it. Automation apps use it to click and type. Because it sees everything, criminals use it to steal bank logins, so Android adds more warnings and limits.

use_cases.example: A blind person uses TalkBack to hear every button read aloud.
A person with limited movement uses Switch Access to control the phone with one button.
An automation app fills in forms and taps buttons for you.
A password manager fills login forms in other apps.
A game helper app taps the screen for you, which many games ban.
Malware reads a bank code from the screen and moves money, which is why it is dangerous.
A support tool lets an agent see and control your screen when you ask for help.

risks: Hard to tell good from bad
story.android_note: Android 13 blocks sideloaded apps from enabling it, and Android 17 hides sensitive fields from non tool services.
story.ios_note: iPhone has no matching tool. Assistive apps use Switch Control or Guided Access.

technical_bounds: Cannot read secure FLAG_SECURE content in all cases

history.change: Advanced Protection blocks non tool accessibility apps

platform.prompt_ui: Settings > Accessibility > Installed apps; full control warning
platform.store_policy: Play: Accessibility API policy (declaration, isAccessibilityTool, 2022)
platform.note: Android 13 restricted settings blocks sideloaded apps from enabling it; Android 17 hides sensitive fields from non-tool services.

capabilities.name: Kiosk and app pinning
capabilities.plain: Locks the phone to one app.
capabilities.meaning: Used for kiosks and exams. Android has screen pinning for users and lock task for device owners; iOS has Guided Access and supervised Single App Mode.

limits.headline: Can lock the phone to one app when you pin it or a company allows it
limits.user_action: You pin the screen, or triple click to start Guided Access
can: Keep you inside one app, like a kiosk or an exam
Hide the status bar and navigation (Android lock task, company set)
Run exam apps in single app mode on supervised iPhones

Use lock task on Android unless the company is the device owner
Use autonomous single app mode on iPhone unless it is supervised
limits.differs: Android has screen pinning for you and lock task for device owners; iPhone has Guided Access and supervised Single App Mode.

story.what_it_is: Locks the phone to a single app, for kiosks, exams and kids.
story.for_you: A pin icon appears and the phone stays on one app. You cannot swipe away until you unlock with a gesture or a code. It feels like a locked room for that app.
story.for_makers: Schools, shops and tests need a phone that cannot wander. Pinning keeps the screen on the task and blocks notifications and the home screen. Fleet owners use a stronger lock mode on company devices.

use_cases.example: A student takes an online exam and cannot open other apps.
A store uses a tablet as a point of sale and it stays on the sales app.
A parent pins a phone to a learning game so a child cannot wander.
An airport kiosk keeps the check in app on screen all day.
A hospital tablet stays on a patient intake form.
A museum game kiosk is locked on the exhibit app.
A phone loan to a stranger is pinned to the phone dialer to make a call.

risks: Hard to exit if you forget the code
story.android_note: Android has screen pinning for users and lock task mode for device owners, which can also hide the status bar and navigation.
story.ios_note: iPhone has Guided Access for users and Single App Mode on supervised devices, used by exam apps.

technical_bounds: Third party apps cannot self pin on unmanaged devices on iOS

platform.permission: None (screen pinning); device owner for lock task
platform.note: Lock task can disable status bar and nav.

capabilities.name: Device admin and Device Policy (work profile, device owner)

capabilities.meaning: Controls passwords, app installs, wiping and cameras. Device admin is deprecated; device owner and work profile are the supported routes.

Control app installs and cameras
Wipe the phone
Keep work data apart in a work profile

Use the old device admin tools on newer Android; many were removed in Android 14
See personal data in an Android work profile

story.what_it_is: Lets a company app enforce rules on a phone, such as password strength, and wipe it if it is lost.

marketing.name: Android Enterprise
marketing.pitch: Android Enterprise lets companies manage work apps and data on phones, from work profiles to fully managed devices.

story.for_you: At work you may be asked to install a management app. After you accept, your boss can set a password rule or wipe the work part of the phone. A work profile keeps personal photos apart.
story.for_makers: Companies need to protect customer data on staff phones. Device admin and the newer device owner and work profile tools let them enforce locks, block installs and remotely wipe. Old device admin is deprecated for new apps.

use_cases.example: A company makes staff use a strong PIN on work phones and wipes the phone if it is lost.
A bank locks a work phone's camera in secure areas.
A school sets up shared tablets with only approved apps.
An airline gives crew work phones that cannot install games.
A hospital limits a phone to approved clinical apps.
A delivery company controls courier phones and updates the app remotely.
A lost phone service locks and wipes your own phone.

story.android_note: Device admin APIs are deprecated since Android 9 and many were removed in Android 14 for apps that are not device owners. Work profile keeps personal data separate.
story.ios_note: iPhone does not use an app API. Control comes through mobile device management profiles.

platform.store_policy: Play: device admin deprecated; DPC policy
platform.note: Device admin APIs deprecated in Android 9 and many removed in 14 for non device owners.

capabilities.name: Mobile device management and supervision

capabilities.meaning: MDM can install apps, set Wi-Fi and VPN, block features and wipe the device. Supervised iOS devices allow tighter control, such as app lockdown and content filters.

limits.headline: Can control settings, apps and restrictions on the phone, once a company enrolls it

Wipe the device

See personal data in an Android work profile
Control the phone without your enrollment steps or Apple Business Manager setup

story.what_it_is: A company server that controls a phone's settings, apps and restrictions.

marketing.name: Device management
marketing.pitch: Apple lets organizations configure, manage and secure iPhones and iPads at scale.

story.for_you: At work or school you tap a link to enroll, and the phone starts to follow rules. Your boss may install apps, set Wi-Fi, block features or wipe the device. With personal phones the work part can be kept apart.
story.for_makers: Companies and schools run thousands of phones from one dashboard. They push apps, set VPN and Wi-Fi, block features, and wipe lost devices. Supervised devices give much more control than personal ones.

use_cases.example: IT sets up a new hire's phone with email, Wi-Fi and the right apps before the first day.
A school locks iPads to learning apps during class.
A hospital pushes a clinical app to every nurse's phone.
An airline updates every pilot's tablet at once.
A courier company installs a route app and blocks other apps on driver phones.
A security team wipes a lost phone from a web page.
A parent uses a family device manager to set up a child's phone.

story.android_note: A work profile keeps personal data apart, while a fully managed device gives the company full control.
story.ios_note: User Enrollment limits what management can see on a personal iPhone. Supervised devices give much broader control.

technical_bounds: Needs enrollment or supervision

platform.prompt_ui: QR provisioning, zero touch, managed Google Play
platform.store_policy: Play: managed Google Play
platform.note: Work profile keeps personal data separate; fully managed gives full control.

story.for_makers: Ad blockers, parental filters and malware guards need to see where traffic goes. The tool can block whole lists of domains. It also sees the sites you visit, so trust in the maker matters.

use_cases.example: A DNS blocker stops phishing and malware sites for the whole phone.
A parent blocks adult sites and social apps on a child's phone.
A blocker removes ads and trackers inside games and news apps.
A company blocks risky categories on staff phones.
A news reader loads faster with ads stripped.
A filter blocks game ad networks so free games play with fewer interruptions.
A privacy app shows which apps call which tracker domains.

story.android_note: Many ad blockers use a local VPN on Android.
story.ios_note: Safari content blockers work on any iPhone. A full network data filter needs a supervised device.

technical_bounds: iOS flow filter limited to supervised devices

platform.permission: Private DNS setting; VpnService for local filters
platform.store_policy: Play: VpnService policy
platform.note: Many ad blockers use a local VPN.

limits.user_action: You open Settings, then Notifications, and switch the app on under Device and app notifications

See other apps' notifications on iPhone

story.what_it_is: Lets an app read what other apps show in your notification shade.
story.for_you: A special setting asks to give an app notification access. If you agree, it can read every notification, including bank codes and private chats. A smartwatch uses it to mirror alerts on your wrist.
story.for_makers: Smartwatch makers, car displays and automation apps need to see alerts. Notification text can hold codes and messages, so a bad app can steal them. That is why Android hides this behind a special switch.

use_cases.example: A smartwatch app mirrors your phone alerts to your wrist.
A car display app reads your messages aloud while you drive.
An automation app turns a delivery alert into a reminder.
A bank code stealing app reads a one time code from a text alert.
A hearing assist app flashes a light when an alert arrives.
A time tracking app counts the notifications from each app.
A home hub says your door bell alert out loud.

story.android_note: Android 13 restricted settings also block sideloaded notification listener apps.
story.ios_note: iPhone does not allow apps to read other apps' notifications.

technical_bounds: iOS limits to accessories and EU

history.change: EU third party accessory notification forwarding

platform.store_policy: Play: user data policy; restricted setting for sideloaded apps
platform.note: Android 13 restricted settings applies to sideloaded listener apps.

capabilities.name: Restricted settings for sideloaded apps
capabilities.plain: Android blocks some powerful toggles for apps installed outside stores.

limits.headline: Can't turn on powerful settings for apps installed outside stores until you allow it
limits.user_action: You open App info, tap the menu and choose Allow restricted settings
can: Install outside a store on Android
Ask you to unlock the options in App info
cannot: Use accessibility or notification listener until you allow restricted settings
Unlock the options by itself
Do this on iPhone; there is no sideloading path on most devices
limits.differs: Android blocks these toggles for sideloaded apps; iPhone has no equivalent.

story.what_it_is: Android blocks powerful toggles for apps installed from outside the store, until you unlock them on purpose.
story.for_you: If you install an app from a website, some switches look greyed out. You have to open App info and allow restricted settings first. It is a speed bump that makes scammers' lives harder.
story.for_makers: Scammers talk people into installing an app and then turning on accessibility or notification access. Restricted settings adds a step that the scammer cannot complete without you noticing. It is a platform level defense against fraud.

use_cases.example: A fake bank app tries to get accessibility access and is blocked until the user unlocks it.
A scam call tells someone to install a support tool, and the greyed out switch breaks the script.
A company sideloads a work app and has to approve it for settings.
A developer testing an app learns why a setting is greyed out.
A game helper app installed from a website cannot get screen tap control.
An anti malware app uses the same switch to protect the person.
A payment fraud team counts how many cases the block stopped.

risks: Hard to use for legitimate sideloaded apps
Users can be coached around it
story.android_note: Android 14 widened the block, Android 15 changed rules for session installers and Android 16 adds more checks.
story.ios_note: Not used on iPhone.

technical_bounds: Apps from Play are exempt

platform.api_surface: Not an app API; PackageInstaller sessions mark source
platform.note: Android 14 expanded the scope; Android 15 refined for session installers; Android 16 more checks.

capabilities.name: App privacy report and Privacy Dashboard
capabilities.plain: A log in Settings showing which apps used sensors and which domains they contacted.
capabilities.meaning: Android's dashboard shows sensor access. Apple's report adds network domains.

limits.headline: Can show you which apps used sensors, and on iPhone which domains they contacted

can: List which apps used location, camera and microphone
Show when each use happened
Show the domains apps contacted (iPhone)
cannot: List contacted domains on Android
Record on iPhone before you switch on Record App Activity
Block or change what apps do; it only shows a log
limits.differs: Android shows sensor access only; iPhone adds network domains.

story.what_it_is: A log in Settings that shows which apps used your camera, mic or location, and which sites they talked to.

marketing.name: App Privacy Report
marketing.pitch: See how apps use the access you gave them, and which websites they contact.

story.for_you: You switch it on in Settings and then read a simple list. You can see which app used the mic last night and which tracker domains it contacted. It is a way to catch an app that is too chatty.
story.for_makers: The report tells honest apps they will be watched. It also gives a public way to expose bad behavior, since a long list of ad domains is easy to spot. Makers must be ready to explain what their apps send.

use_cases.example: A journalist checks which apps contacted unknown domains.
A parent looks at which apps used the camera on a child's phone.
A free game is found to contact dozens of ad domains.
A privacy researcher compares an app's promises with its network contacts.
A developer checks that their own SDKs do not contact surprise domains.
A person finds that a health app read their location overnight.
IT checks that work apps contact only approved sites.

story.android_note: Android's dashboard shows sensor use, such as location, camera and microphone, with no list of domains.
story.ios_note: Apple's report also lists the domains each app contacted.

technical_bounds: Reports are user facing only

platform.persistence: 24 hours at launch; 7 days from Android 15 QPR1
platform.note: Location, camera, microphone; no domain list

capabilities.name: Unused app permission reset
capabilities.plain: Automatically removes permissions from apps not opened for months.
capabilities.meaning: Limits dormant exposure. Android resets runtime permissions after about three months unused; iOS has no automatic revocation.

limits.headline: Can remove permissions from apps you have not opened for about three months, on Android
limits.user_action: Nothing. Android does it on its own and sends you a notice
can: Reset the permissions of apps you stopped using
Tell you when a reset happens
Apply to apps built for Android 11 and later by default, and older ones through Google Play services
cannot: Do this on iPhone; it never removes permissions by itself
Reset permissions for apps you keep opening
Replace your own choices in Settings
limits.differs: Android resets unused app permissions after about three months; iPhone only reminds you now and then about location.

story.what_it_is: Automatically takes away permissions from apps you have not opened for months.

marketing.name: Permission auto reset
marketing.pitch: Android removes permissions from apps you have not used in a few months, and tells you.

story.for_you: If you have not opened an app for about three months, its permissions go away. You get a notice and can turn them back on. You never need to clean up old apps yourself.
story.for_makers: Dormant apps keep access forever, which is a risk. Auto reset cuts that exposure. Makers have to ask again when the person returns, so they need a good reason to win trust back.

use_cases.example: A game you played last summer loses location access and asks again when you open it.
A holiday shopping app loses camera access until you come back in winter.
A trip app that you used once loses its location permission.
A fitness app you forgot about loses health data access.
An old social app loses its contacts access.
A tracking SDK inside a stale app loses its sensor access.
A security team sees fewer old permissions across a fleet of phones.

story.android_note: Applies to apps for Android 11 and later by default, and was backported to Android 6 through Play services in 2021 and 2022.
story.ios_note: iPhone never takes permissions away on its own. It reminds you now and then about location use.

technical_bounds: No iOS equivalent

history.change: Auto-reset backported via Google Play services

platform.persistence: Resets after a few months unused; app hibernates
platform.store_policy: Play: apps must not circumvent
platform.note: Applies to apps targeting API 30 and later by default; backported to 6.0 via Play services in 2021-22.

story.what_it_is: Lets an app read and change your Do Not Disturb settings.
story.for_you: A special switch asks to let the app control Do Not Disturb. If you allow it, a meeting app can silence your phone for you. A bedtime app can turn it on at night.
story.for_makers: Apps that care about sleep, meetings and focus want to flip the setting for you. Reading it also tells them if you are busy. On iPhone it is only a yes or no.

use_cases.example: A calendar app turns on Do Not Disturb during your meetings.
A sleep app silences notifications at bedtime and turns them back on in the morning.
A workout app silences calls so a run is not interrupted.
A study timer blocks alerts during a study session.
A driving app turns on Do Not Disturb while you drive.
A parent app sets quiet time at school.
A game silences notifications during a match.

story.android_note: Android needs special access to change the interruption filter.
story.ios_note: iPhone only returns a yes or no for whether a Focus is on and cannot change it.

A school sets homework mode that blocks social apps.
A digital wellbeing app shows you how long you used social media today.
A parent sets a bedtime lock on a child's game console style apps.
A teen asks their parent to approve a new chat app.
A parent blocks adult sites for a child.
An adult sets their own limits to reduce doom scrolling.

A developer tests how an app behaves when features are off.

cannot: Be fully unique for every phone; some phones look the same
Look up an ID you can see or clear in settings
Get as many signals on iPhone; Apple limits what apps can learn
Stay the same after a system update changes one of the signals
limits.differs: Android shows apps more hardware detail. iPhone offers fewer signals, but timestamps and settings can still be used.

story.what_it_is: Mixing many small phone details into a guess that is close to unique.
story.for_you: You never see it. Even if you turn off the ad ID, your phone's model, language, screen and other small facts can add up to a tag that follows you. Apple bans this for people who said no to tracking.
story.for_makers: Makers and ad firms use it to count people when no ID is allowed, and to spot fraud and bots. It is accurate but breaks easily, and app stores treat the tracking use as a policy violation.

use_cases.example: An ad measurement tool matches an ad click to an install by comparing device details when the ad ID is off.
A bank notices a login from a phone with a new fingerprint and asks for an extra check.
A game spots a farm of fake devices with identical settings that claim sign up bonuses.
A store ties a new session to a returning shopper after cookies and IDs are wiped.
A payment company scores risk by how much a device looks like known fraud devices.
A tool counts unique phones from sets of signals without reading any ID.

story.android_note: Android does not ban it in the same way, but Google Play rules restrict it for ads.
story.ios_note: Apple rejects apps that fingerprint people who refused tracking.

technical_bounds: Apple review blocks it for ATT-denied users
Android allows non-ad uses

history.change: Required reason APIs target fingerprint inputs

platform.store_policy: Play: persistent IDs only for non-ad uses; Data safety must declare

capabilities.name: Hashed email and phone identity graphs (UID2, RampID)
capabilities.plain: Ad firms turn a hashed email or phone into a shared ID that follows people across apps and sites.
capabilities.meaning: When device IDs are blocked, a login or email is the best key. Graphs link logins to ads across publishers, and they rely on the person having signed in.

data.metric: SHA-256 email or phone to UID2 or RampID token

limits.headline: Can match you across apps and sites using your email or phone, scrambled into an ID
limits.user_action: You sign in or give your email or phone to an app or site
can: Turn your email or phone into a scrambled code and share that code with ad partners
Recognize you in other apps and websites that use the same system
Work on both Android and iPhone through ad SDKs and server to server links
cannot: Match you if you never give an email or phone to any partner
Match you when you use Hide My Email; Apple's relay address breaks the link
Use your real email directly; partners share the scrambled version
Work after you opt out where the ID provider offers an opt out
limits.reach_label: Follows you across apps and sites
limits.differs: Hide My Email on iPhone can break matching. Android sign in gives apps your real email.

story.what_it_is: Ad companies turn your email or phone into a shared scrambled ID that follows you across apps and sites.

marketing.name: UID2
marketing.pitch: Pitch: an open ID built from an email or phone that lets advertisers reach people on the open internet with privacy controls.

story.for_you: You type your email to read an article or sign in to a shopping app. Later, ads on other apps and sites may seem to know you. You never see the scrambled ID that links them.
story.for_makers: With device IDs fading, a login is the best key for ads. Publishers sell logged in audiences, and advertisers match their customer lists to them. It only works when people sign in.

use_cases.example: A news site asks you to sign in with an email, then sells ad space to brands that can recognize you by a scrambled copy of it.
A retailer uploads its customer list to an ad network so you see its ads on other apps.
A streaming service lets advertisers reach logged in viewers across phone and TV.
A brand measures whether a TV ad made a known customer buy later in an app.
A game with a login shares a hashed email with an ad partner to find look alike players.
Fraud teams check if one hashed email is tied to hundreds of fake sign ups.

risks: Follows you across apps and sites
story.android_note: Works the same way on Android, with the ad ID as one more signal.
story.ios_note: Works on iPhone too. Sign in with Apple's hidden email stops it.

technical_bounds: Needs a signed-in user
Consent regimes apply
Apple relay emails cannot be matched

abuse: Linking users across apps without disclosure

history.change: ATT pushes advertisers to log-in-based IDs
Mobile SDKs released for Android and iOS

platform.store_policy: Data safety: sharing; User Data policy
platform.api_surface: UID2 SDK, LiveRamp ATS, ID5, server-side APIs
platform.note: Matching uses normalized, hashed email or phone.

capabilities.name: Sign in with Apple and Hide My Email
capabilities.plain: Apple signs the person in and can give the app a random relay email instead of the real one.
capabilities.meaning: Stops the app from using email as a cross-site key; hash matching in UID2 and RampID fails against relay addresses.

data.metric: Stable per-team user ID and optional relay email

limits.headline: Can sign you in on iPhone and give the app a random relay email instead
limits.user_action: You tap Sign in with Apple and choose Share My Email or Hide My Email
can: Sign you in with your Apple account
Give the app your real email, if you pick Share My Email
Give the app a random relay address, if you pick Hide My Email
Forward the app's emails to you through Apple's relay
cannot: Reveal your real email when you pick Hide My Email
Send email to you unless the developer registered its sending domain with Apple
Work on Android; Google Sign-In and Credential Manager return the real email
limits.differs: iPhone only. Android sign in always returns your real email.

story.what_it_is: Apple signs you in and can give the app a random fake email that forwards to you.

marketing.name: Sign in with Apple and Hide My Email
marketing.pitch: Pitch: sign in quickly and keep your real email private with a random address that forwards to you.

marketing.name: Hide My Email
marketing.pitch: Support page: create unique random email addresses that forward to your inbox, so you do not share your real one.

story.for_you: You tap Sign in with Apple, use Face ID, and pick Hide My Email. The app gets a random address that forwards to you. You can turn it off any time, which stops that app's emails.
story.for_makers: Makers get a fast sign up with less typing and fewer fake accounts. They lose the real email as a way to link people across ads and sites, and they must send mail through Apple's relay.

use_cases.example: You sign up for a store and give it a random address, so a data leak or sale of its list never exposes your real email.
A game offers Sign in with Apple so you start in seconds and keep your email private.
A newsletter site uses the relay so you can cut off emails with one tap in Settings.
A dating app lets you sign up without sharing your main email or phone.
An ad firm cannot match a relay address to the same person's other accounts.
Apple's sign in lowers fake account sign ups because each one needs a real Apple account.

risks: Apps may force an Apple account
story.android_note: Android has no matching feature. Google offers its own Sign in with Google with real emails.
story.ios_note: Built into iOS and Apple accounts. Developers must offer it when they offer other social sign ins.

technical_bounds: Real name only on first sign in
Relay needs sender registration

legit_uses: Account creation without handing out an email
abuse: Marketing with a real email via consent

history.change: Sign in with Apple and Hide My Email
Token revocation required for account deletion (30 June 2022)

platform.note: Credential Manager and Google Sign-In return the real email.

capabilities.name: iCloud Private Relay and in-app traffic
capabilities.plain: iCloud Private Relay hides the IP in Safari and some cleartext traffic, but not most app traffic.
capabilities.meaning: Click-side IPs from Safari differ from the app's own IP, hurting probabilistic matching. Apps still see the real IP in their own requests.

limits.headline: Can't hide your IP in most iPhone app traffic, only in Safari and some other traffic
limits.user_action: Nothing. You turn iCloud Private Relay on in iPhone settings
can: Hide your real IP in Safari browsing when you have it on
Hide DNS lookups and unencrypted app web traffic
Give you the same coverage on your iPhone, iPad and Mac with iCloud+
cannot: Hide your IP in most app traffic; secure app connections go direct
Work on Android; use a VPN or Private DNS there
Stop the app from seeing your account, device ID or what you type
Cover everything; Apple's own service decides what goes through
limits.differs: Private Relay is an iPhone feature with iCloud+. Android has no equivalent; people use a VPN or Private DNS.

story.what_it_is: Apple hides your network address in Safari, but most app traffic is not covered.

marketing.name: iCloud Private Relay
marketing.pitch: Pitch: when you browse in Safari, your IP address and browsing activity are protected so no one can build a profile of you.

story.for_you: With Private Relay on, websites in Safari see only a rough region instead of your real address. Most apps still see your real network address, so they can still know roughly where you are.
story.for_makers: Makers who count on IP addresses for ads, fraud checks and install matching find Safari clicks harder to link to app opens. Inside their own apps, they still see the real address, so most tools keep working.

use_cases.example: An install tracker wanted to match a Safari ad click to an app open by network address, but the two now show different addresses.
A bank wanted to flag a login from a far city using the network address. Relay hides the real one in Safari, so it relies on other checks.
A streaming site that blocks by country sees a nearby relay address and may allow or block the wrong people.
A web game with regional servers picks a server by region instead of exact location.
A store that sets prices by city sees only a coarse area from Safari.
A news site that counts unique visitors by address sees groups, not single people.

risks: Gives a false sense of full cover
story.android_note: Android has no matching built in Google feature that hides your address for all browsing.
story.ios_note: A paid iCloud+ feature. It covers Safari, unencrypted app traffic and some DNS, not most app traffic.

technical_bounds: Real IP visible to HTTPS app traffic
Safari click and app IP mismatch

history.change: iCloud Private Relay (beta) launched with iCloud+

platform.note: Android has no Private Relay equivalent; VPN or Private DNS only.

capabilities.name: Shared Keychain access groups and app groups
capabilities.plain: Apps from one developer team can share secrets and files; other developers cannot join.
capabilities.meaning: Lets one company recognize the same person across its own apps. It cannot see another company's keychain items.

limits.headline: Can share saved secrets and files between apps from the same developer on iPhone
limits.user_action: Nothing. The developer sets this up before the app ships
can: Share a login or token between apps from one Apple developer team
Share files and settings through an app group folder
Keep sign in working across a family of apps from the same maker
Share on Android only between apps signed with the same key
cannot: Let apps from other developers join the group
Share across teams; the group name starts with the team prefix
Use sharedUserId on new Android apps; it was deprecated in Android 10
Share on Android with no setup; it needs matching signing keys and a provider
limits.differs: iPhone has built in groups. Android has no direct match and uses same signature sharing.

story.what_it_is: Lets apps from one company on the same phone share passwords, tokens and files.

marketing.name: App Groups
marketing.pitch: Developer guide: let apps from the same team share containers and data on one device.

story.for_you: You sign in once and your other apps from the same company already know you. The upside is smooth use. The downside is that one company can link all of its apps to you without asking.
story.for_makers: Makers use it for single sign on, shared settings and shared downloads between their own apps. Other companies cannot join the group, so it is a safe lane between a developer's own apps.

use_cases.example: You sign in to a mail app and its calendar app from the same company opens already signed in.
A studio shares your save file between its main game and a companion app.
A bank shares a secure login token between its main app and a small widget app.
A music app shares downloaded songs with its car and watch helper apps.
A company shares one login across its work apps so staff sign in once.
A developer uses a shared ID to see that one person uses three of its apps.

story.android_note: Android uses shared user IDs and signing keys for a similar feature, now rarely allowed.
story.ios_note: Needs an Apple entitlement and the same developer team, with no prompt to you.

technical_bounds: Same team only
Requires entitlement

abuse: Cross-app ID inside a brand's family of apps

refs.label: Apple: Sharing access to keychain items

platform.api_surface: android:sharedUserId (deprecated API 29), signature permissions, shared content providers
platform.note: No direct match. Same signing key apps can share through providers.

capabilities.name: Keychain and Block Store persistence across reinstall
capabilities.plain: A stored ID that survives uninstall, so a reinstalled app recognizes the person.
capabilities.meaning: iOS Keychain entries remain after the app is deleted. Android needs Block Store or Auto Backup. Used for fraud and abuse limits, and sometimes tracking.

limits.headline: Can recognize you after a reinstall using an ID that stays behind on your phone
limits.user_action: Nothing. The app saves it quietly the first time you use it
can: Keep an ID in the iPhone Keychain that stays after you delete the app
Keep an ID in Android Block Store or Auto Backup that may come back
Sync the saved item to a new device if iCloud Keychain or Google backup is on
Tell the app you are a returning user
cannot: Share the ID with apps from other developers on iPhone
Survive on Android without backup or Block Store; a normal uninstall clears app data
Stay on a phone after a full wipe or reset
Come back on Android if you turn off backup
limits.differs: iPhone keeps Keychain items after uninstall by default. Android clears them unless backup or Block Store is used.

story.what_it_is: A stored ID that stays after you delete and reinstall the app.

marketing.name: Block Store
marketing.pitch: Developer pitch: keep sign in data across app reinstalls and new devices, with no extra login steps.

story.for_you: You delete an app to start fresh, reinstall it, and it says Welcome back. You will not see the stored ID that told it who you were, and clearing it is not simple.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to stop abuse like repeat free trials, and to keep a person signed in after a reset. Ad and analytics firms also use it to keep a stable ID when the ad ID is blocked.

use_cases.example: A game recognizes a banned cheater who deleted the game and reinstalled, and blocks them again.
A streaming app limits a free trial to once per phone, even after you reinstall.
A store sees your welcome coupon was already used on this phone and does not give it again.
A bank app keeps your device trusted after an update, without a new text code.
A dating app spots someone returning after a ban and stops the new account.
An ad partner joins your pre and post reinstall activity, so attribution stays accurate.

story.android_note: Needs Block Store or Auto Backup. Data can also move to a new phone.
story.ios_note: Keychain items often remain after the app is deleted, unless the developer clears them.

technical_bounds: Apple: only same team; Android: Block Store is per app
Privacy label must declare any identifier collected

history.change: Block Store API released for credentials and IDs

platform.api_surface: Auto Backup (6.0), Block Store (Play services 2022), AccountManager
platform.note: Cleared on uninstall otherwise; backups may restore app data on a new device.

capabilities.name: Mail Privacy Protection and Link Tracking Protection
capabilities.plain: Apple Mail preloads email images through a proxy and Safari and Mail strip known tracking parameters from links.
capabilities.meaning: Open pixels look like opens even when no human saw the email, so email-to-app funnels are noisy. Link Tracking Protection (iOS 17) removes known click IDs from URLs in Mail, Messages and Safari private browsing.

limits.user_action: Nothing. You turn it on in Mail settings and Safari uses it by default
can: Preload email images through Apple's proxy so open tracking is hidden
Strip known tracking tags from links in Safari and Mail on iOS 17 and newer
Hide your IP from the sender when it loads the images
cannot: Strip custom tracking tags, only known ones such as gclid, fbclid and mc_eid
Work in Gmail or other Android mail apps; no matching system feature exists
Stop a sender from knowing you clicked a link they sent
Hide that an email was delivered
limits.differs: This is Apple Mail and Safari only. Android and Gmail have no system wide match.

story.what_it_is: Apple Mail hides when you open an email and strips tracking codes from links.

marketing.name: Mail Privacy Protection
marketing.pitch: Pitch: stops senders from learning if you opened their email and hides your IP address from them.

story.for_you: Marketing emails can no longer tell when you read them or where you are. Links you tap in Mail, Messages and private Safari lose some tracking codes, so what you click is harder to trace.
story.for_makers: Open rates now look high even when no human read the email, so email to app funnels are noisy. Makers lean on clicks, app opens and sign ins instead of the open pixel.

use_cases.example: An advertiser wanted to retarget people who opened its email. Apple Mail now preloads images, so everyone looks like an opener.
A store wanted to send a follow up to people who opened a deal email, and now relies on actual clicks.
A newsletter wanted to find the most engaged readers and now counts link clicks and app opens.
A growth team wanted to see which email led to an app install, and now uses clean links and app events.
A game wanted to email lapsed players if they opened a comeback offer, and now uses push messages.
Phishing senders lose the ability to confirm that a real person opened a scam email.

risks: Marketers may switch to harder tracking
story.android_note: Gmail hides your address by proxying images, but it does not preload every email like Apple Mail does.

technical_bounds: Custom params survive
Universal links pass through unchanged

capabilities.plain: An MMP guesses which ad click led to an install by matching IP, device model and OS version within a short time window.
capabilities.meaning: Without IDs, the vendor matches the click (IP, UA, language, OS) with the first app open from the same signals, usually within hours. Apple treats this as fingerprinting for ATT-denied users.

story.what_it_is: A guess about which ad led to an install, made by comparing network and device details.
story.for_you: You tap an ad, install the app and the ad firm quietly matches the two by network address and device details. You never see this. It can be wrong, especially on shared Wi-Fi.
story.for_makers: When IDs are blocked, ad firms still need to say which campaign worked. Matching in a short window gives an estimate for budgets. Apple treats it as fingerprinting when the person said no to tracking.

use_cases.example: A game studio checks which of five video ads brought a new player, using the click and first open from the same Wi-Fi.
A retailer measures whether an influencer link caused app installs.
A mobile game pays an ad network per install, and the match decides who gets paid.
Fraud teams spot clicks that claim installs by guessing from the same address at odd hours.
A booking app estimates which search ad led to its first booking in the app.
A marketing team compares the guess to Apple's own aggregate ad reports.

story.android_note: Allowed more freely, though Google Play rules limit ad use.

Not allowed on iOS for denied users per Apple
